procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 16, 1963 of the Madras High Court in Criminal Revision Case No. 1139 of 1961 (Criminal Revision Petition No. 1095 of 1961).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant took the matter in revision to the Madras High Court, but the revision application was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment of the Madras High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant is illegal because six items of alleged cheating were combined together in one charge.

facts: The lower courts had previously found that all six items of cheating were not separate incidents but were 'part and parcel of one transaction'.
law: Section 239 of the Criminal Procedure Code permits the trial of an accused on a single charge for multiple offenses if those offenses are part of the same transaction.
application: The Supreme Court accepted the lower courts' finding that the six acts of cheating constituted a single transaction.
Because the acts were part of one transaction, the Court determined that trying them under a single charge was permissible according to Section 239 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the conviction was not illegal because combining the six items of cheating into one charge was legally permissible since they were all part of the same transaction.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a breach of s. 361, Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The appellant contended that the evidence of prosecution witnesses was given in Tamil or English, neither of which he understood.
The appellant was represented in the trial court by two eminent advocates who knew both languages.
The appellant did not make any objection at the time the evidence was being given in court.
law: Section 361(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code states that whenever evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused, it shall be interpreted to him in a language he understands.
Section 537 of the Criminal Procedure Code allows for procedural irregularities to be cured if they have not resulted in any injustice.
application: The Court assumed for the sake of argument that the appellant did not know English or Tamil.
It characterized the potential violation of s. 361(1) as "merely an irregularity."
The Court found that no prejudice was caused to the appellant on this account.
This lack of prejudice was supported by the fact that his two eminent lawyers knew the languages and would have protected his interests.
Because the irregularity did not result in any injustice, the Court held that the defect was curable under the provisions of s. 537.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that even if there was a breach of s. 361, it was a curable irregularity that did not cause any prejudice to the appellant and therefore did not vitiate the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a breach of s. 361, Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: There was a breach of s. 361, Criminal Procedure Code, as the trial was conducted in Tamil and English, neither of which the appellant knew.
respondent_arguments: The appellant was represented by eminent counsel, and no prejudice was caused to him by the languages used in the trial.
Any breach of s. 361 was only a procedural irregularity that is curable under s. 537 of the Code.

cases.principle: To establish the legal position of a 'pucca adatia', which is that they act as a principal in relation to their constituent and not as an agent, and that there is no privity of contract between the upcountry constituent and the Bombay merchant.

cases.case_name: Bhagwandas Parasram v. Burjorji Ruttonji Bomanji
cases.principle: To affirm the legal principle that a 'pucca adatia' is not an agent of their constituent but acts as a principal in the transaction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A pucca adatia has no authority to pledge the credit of an upcountry constituent to a merchant, as there is no privity of contract between the upcountry constituent and the merchant.
obiter: A forward contract for goods in a specified area, conducted otherwise than between members of a recognized association or through such a member, is illegal.
The trial of an appellant on a single charge is permissible under s. 239, Criminal Procedure Code, when the acts in question are part and parcel of one transaction.

The lower courts correctly determined that all six items of cheating were integral parts of a single transaction, which therefore permitted them to be tried together under a single charge as allowed by s. 239 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
